edits.purpose: Remove the repeated opening question and itinerary; leave the Key Ideas box unchanged and put the argument immediately after it.
edits.original:
What happens to the software factory when agents substantially increase its capacity for realization?

To answer that question, this chapter begins with an older change in production. The Industrial Revolution did more than increase the power available to make things. It changed how production was controlled. As machinery increased the rate of fabrication, engineers developed ways to organize production and to specify and measure the bounds within which its products had to remain.

This chapter develops the software factory from that history and then examines contemporary agentic software factories. DocAble provides a case observed from the inside, including how its factory changed as production accelerated. Public accounts from other organizations show how different factories divide realization and supervision under different constraints.

edits.purpose: Establish the change of unit from engineering episodes to the production system, then motivate history and the complementary cases.
edits.original: \magevalue{sec:the-software-factory} develops the software-factory concept from the history of manufacturing and asks what a production system must know and control when fabrication outruns direct human supervision. \magevalue{sec:inside-docables-software-factory} examines DocAble from the inside, tracing how its engineering structures changed with its capacity for realization. \magevalue{sec:mage-in-the-wild} compares other organizations through their reported mechanisms, measurements, and operating decisions. The coda returns to process design, tolerance, and engineering authority, preparing the questions about cost and reliability developed in \magevalue{chapter:theory}.
edits.replacement:
\magevalue{chapter:one-problem-many-models} followed Modeling and Alignment through individual engineering episodes, showing how representations and controls changed as DocAble evolved. We now widen the view from those episodes to the production system that made them possible. An agent may implement a change, but the surrounding factory determines how work is selected, what knowledge reaches the agent, which decisions remain open, how results are evaluated, and when a change may be accepted.

The Industrial Revolution offers a useful comparison. It did more than increase the power available to fabricate things. It changed how production was organized and controlled. As machinery increased the rate of fabrication, engineers developed production processes, standards, and measurements that allowed work to proceed without continuous supervision of every operation. The factory became an engineered system in its own right.

This chapter examines the corresponding change in software engineering. \magevalue{sec:the-software-factory} develops two concerns of factory engineering: process design, which organizes production, and tolerance, which establishes acceptable variation in what is produced. \magevalue{sec:inside-docables-software-factory} examines DocAble's factory from the inside, tracing its development, operating mechanisms, and measured results. \magevalue{sec:mage-in-the-wild} then examines factories developed independently by other organizations. These accounts show how the same engineering concerns lead to different arrangements when organizations have different systems, personnel, and obligations.

edits.purpose: Explain why the longitudinal DocAble case and public industrial accounts provide complementary evidence rather than merely announcing the route.

\magevalue{sec:inside-docables-software-factory} follows these questions through DocAble as its realization capacity grows; \magevalue{sec:mage-in-the-wild} uses them to examine different arrangements reported by other organizations.
edits.replacement:
% <!-- point: the-four-questions-are-broader-than-mage | A longitudinal case explains development and mechanisms, while public industrial accounts expose variation in the allocation of work, authority, and control. -->

These questions can be answered at different levels of detail. A longitudinal account can show how a factory's arrangements developed, which problems prompted changes, and what the resulting machinery accomplished. Reports from established organizations can show how factories differ in their allocation of work, authority, and control, although they rarely expose the same development history. DocAble provides the first perspective; the industrial accounts provide the second.

edits.purpose: Lead with the coupled product/factory problem, then retain governed measurements and authorial decisions before applying process design and tolerance.
edits.original:
% <!-- point: one-engineer-directed-a-fleet | One engineer directed coding agents over the 31 complete weeks examined; the final snapshot contains 615,395 production lines, 2,333,471 apparatus lines, and 143 model modules. | terms: fleet-scale -->

DocAble was built by one engineer (me) directing a fleet of coding agents. The record examined here spans \magevalue{seip_weeks} complete weeks, from March 12 through October 14, 2026. At the final snapshot, the system contained \magevalue{seip_prod_loc} lines of production code and \magevalue{seip_apparatus_loc} lines of engineering apparatus, including tests, checks, tools, infrastructure, models, and indexed documentation. The history identified \magevalue{seip_models} model modules. These measurements describe the resulting software and its engineering environment; they do not measure how much useful work each line or model represents.

% <!-- point: the-engineers-role-was-engineering-not-implementation | Goals, users, production failures, standards and institutional use supplied engineering work; the engineer made the consequential decisions. | terms: governed-engineering-environment -->

New work came from my goals for the system, user feedback, production failures, accessibility standards, public guidance from advocacy groups,\citep{nfb-accessible-documents-2014} and the demands of institutional use. I decided which pressures warranted engineering work and made consequential decisions about requirements, architecture, validation, and deployment. Agents performed most of the implementation. I inspected almost none of the code they produced.

% <!-- point: product-decisions-became-factory-obligations | The product and its engineering environment developed together: product decisions became obligations governing later agent changes. -->

I was engineering two coupled systems: DocAble and the factory that produced it. The product had to improve accessibility while preserving the document properties its users depended on. Its architecture expressed decisions about how to satisfy those requirements; the factory had to preserve the decisions as agents changed the implementation. A failure could therefore require two repairs: changing the product and changing how future work on it was governed.

% <!-- point: the-division-of-work-is-the-factory-examined | The case connects the build record to mature models and workflow, selected conversions, supervisory work, product results and liabilities. -->

The case follows that development from the requirements and build record into the mature factory: what it represents, how work proceeds, and how selected failures changed its machinery. It then examines the engineer's changing role and the product's measured results. The chronology matters because the environment did not arrive fully formed. It developed as implementation, institutional use, and observed failures exposed engineering decisions that needed to persist.

% <!-- point: one-engineer-directed-a-fleet | One engineer directed coding agents while engineering both the remediation product and its factory; the final snapshot records production source, supporting source, and model modules. | terms: fleet-scale -->

DocAble was built by one engineer (me) directing a fleet of coding agents. The product was a document-accessibility remediation service; the factory was the production system through which I directed changes to that service. I was engineering both. The product had to improve accessibility while preserving the document properties its users depended on. The factory had to organize implementation and preserve consequential engineering decisions as agents changed the system.

The record examined here spans \magevalue{seip_weeks} complete weeks, from March 12 through October 14, 2026. At the final snapshot, DocAble contained \magevalue{seip_prod_loc} lines of production code and \magevalue{seip_apparatus_loc} lines of supporting source, including tests, checks, tools, infrastructure, models, and indexed documentation. The history identified \magevalue{seip_models} model modules. These measurements describe the resulting system and its engineering environment; they do not measure how much useful work each line or model represents.

% <!-- point: the-engineers-role-was-engineering-not-implementation | Goals, users, production failures, standards and institutional use supplied engineering work; the engineer made consequential decisions while coding agents wrote every implementation line. | terms: governed-engineering-environment -->

New work came from my goals for the system, user feedback, production failures, accessibility standards, public guidance from advocacy groups\citep{nfb-accessible-documents-2014}, and the demands of institutional use. I decided which pressures warranted engineering work and made consequential decisions about requirements, architecture, validation, and deployment. Coding agents wrote every line of the implementation. I inspected almost none of the code they produced.

% <!-- point: product-decisions-became-factory-obligations | Process design organized work and tolerance preserved consequential requirements while agents retained implementation freedom; failures could require changes to both the product and its factory. -->

That division of work required process design and tolerance. Work had to be selected, planned, dispatched, integrated, and evaluated without making me the bottleneck for every implementation decision. At the same time, agents needed freedom to choose implementations without being free to violate consequential requirements. The factory therefore developed models, procedures, tools, and controls that carried selected decisions into later work. A failure could require two repairs: changing the product and changing how future changes to it were governed.

% <!-- point: the-division-of-work-is-the-factory-examined | The case follows factory development from initial requirements through production operation; implementation, institutional use, and observed failures exposed engineering decisions that needed to persist. -->

The case follows the factory's development from initial requirements through production operation. Its chronology matters because the machinery did not arrive fully formed. Implementation, institutional use, and observed failures exposed engineering decisions that needed to persist; the factory changed to carry them.

As DocAble grew, source code alone stopped being an adequate engineering interface. Repository search could locate a symbol without explaining which services participated in a workflow, who owned a piece of state, or which resource bound a proposed change had to preserve. The mature factory maintains representations that answer those questions and connects them to the work that depends on them.

As DocAble grew, source code alone stopped being an adequate engineering interface. Repository search could locate a symbol without explaining which services participated in a workflow, who owned a piece of state, or which resource bound a proposed change had to preserve. The growth in supporting source recorded in \autoref{support-ratio-curve} reflects my response to such problems. The following examples show what that investment made possible: representations that answered engineering questions directly, relationships from which the factory could derive checks and configuration, and controls that made selected obligations consequential for later changes.

edits.purpose: Make the industrial comparison arise from the DocAble evidence and its costs, without claiming independent validation of MAGE.
edits.original:
% <!-- point: turn-outward-to-other-factories | The transition: DocAble is one deliberately engineered response to abundant realization, so a factory has to be evaluated as a production system rather than by agent capability alone; the next question is whether independently developed factories exhibit the same pressures. -->

DocAble shows one deliberately engineered response to abundant realization. The factory therefore has to be evaluated as a production system, including the structures that direct and supervise realization, rather than by agent capability alone. The next question is whether independently developed agentic software factories exhibit the same pressures --- and that question does not depend on anyone else having heard of MAGE.
edits.replacement:
% <!-- point: turn-outward-to-other-factories | DocAble's organization of production and preservation of obligations incurred maintenance costs; public accounts can show whether related problems and responses recur under different organizational conditions. -->

DocAble shows how one software factory developed as implementation capacity increased. The resulting machinery addressed two related concerns: organizing production so that agents could perform substantial work without requiring continuous human supervision, and preserving selected product and engineering obligations as that work proceeded. The case also shows the cost of these arrangements. Models, checks, and procedures had to be created, connected to implementation, and maintained as the system changed.

Those observations raise a broader question. Were these problems peculiar to DocAble and its one-engineer development process, or were other organizations encountering similar pressures as they introduced agents into software production? The public accounts examined next describe factories built under different organizational conditions. They cannot provide the same longitudinal evidence, but they can show whether the engineering problems and responses identified here appear elsewhere.

edits.purpose: Add admission authority before the existing supervisory-capacity and carrying-cost comparison, using the reported scope of four existing cases.
edits.original: % <!-- point: supervision-and-verification-do-not-scale-with-production | Production and supervisory capacity can grow at different rates; review delays, workload scheduling, and verification experience make this a process-design concern. -->
edits.replacement:
One important difference is where the authority to accept work resides. Cloudflare distinguishes standards that advise reviewers from those whose violations can block a merge, while retaining a recorded human override\citep{skidmore2026review}. Spotify inserted agents into an existing production process but kept required verification and, in the reported configuration, human review of agent-authored changes\citep{charas2025honk,curtis2026spotifyqcon}. Shopify's security workflow reserves merge authority to the engineers responsible for the affected code\citep{son2026security}; GitLab's documented security-review flow can report findings but cannot approve a change\citep{gitlab2026securityreview}. These arrangements reserve admission authority in different ways, but none treats the producing agent's claim of completion as sufficient authority to admit consequential changes. Process design determines who or what may make the admission decision; tolerance and its evidence determine what that decision must establish.

edits.purpose: Conclude with the factory as an engineered arrangement and let the unchanged process-design/tolerance paragraph provide the payoff.
edits.original:
% <!-- point: process-design-and-tolerance-describe-the-differences-without-a-maturity-model | The cases expose different arrangements of knowledge, production, evaluation, and authority rather than stages of a common maturity sequence. | terms: tolerance -->

The factories in this chapter arrange engineering knowledge, production, evaluation, and authority in different ways. DocAble provides a close account of how those arrangements developed within one project; the public cases show other choices under different organizational conditions. Some preserve obligations in explicit representations, some organize access to existing knowledge, and some change how work reaches review and admission. Their reported outcomes remain uneven, but their mechanisms make the choices concrete. They give engineers alternatives to examine, rather than stages of a common maturity sequence.
edits.replacement:
% <!-- point: process-design-and-tolerance-describe-the-differences-without-a-maturity-model | A software factory arranges engineering knowledge, production capacity, evidence, and authority; those choices determine delegation, protected obligations, and the next production constraint. | terms: tolerance -->

The software factory is an arrangement of engineering knowledge, production capacity, evidence, and authority. The cases in this chapter show that these elements can be organized in substantially different ways. A factory may rely on explicit models, inherited organizational procedures, human reviewers, independent checks, or combinations of them. Those choices determine how much implementation can be delegated, which obligations remain protected, and where additional production capacity encounters its next constraint.
